title: The Third Name
passages:
Márk stood beside the stone panel, heart hammering. The silver trace on his palm pulsed once, then dimmed. He closed his eyes and whispered 'Márk'. The ledger bled black ink across the vellum, the toll climbing to ninety‑one. The cord that bound the book’s spine tightened around his claimed hand and then released, leaving a faint shimmer on his skin. Wall‑voice rose from the corridor, its tone softer than before: 'The keeper pays, the keeper remembers, but the hand forgets what it writes.' Sára watched from the doorway, her throat empty of the first memory of Ilka, feeling the weight of the toll settle on her shoulders.

Ákos heard the shift and felt his lullaby falter. He tried to sing 'Mother', but each note drained a fragment of his recollection of her. The cord tugged toward his throat, and the claimed hand trembled, losing the silver script it had written moments ago. He clutched his chest, aware that every name spoken was a coin taken from his past.

Ilka stepped onto the panel, warm breath against the stone, and the cold dissolved completely. The ledger froze at ninety‑one, a soft chime ringing as the cord on the claimed hand snapped free, dropping the trace onto the floor. From the far end of the corridor a low murmur drifted: 'Listen, and you shall hear the water's mark.' A narrow stair curled downward, leading to the riverbank where the current whispered promises of washing the toll away.

The stair took them down through cold stone and then into damp air. At the bottom, the riverbank was a shelf of black rock slick with moss. The water lapped at the foot of the stone beneath the ledger and, where the current met it, pushed back in thin hard lines, writing letters in the shallow dark. The first line was made of old names: MÁRK, then ILKA, then SÁRA. Ilka read them from the water with her warm eyes, and the cold that had clung to the ledger began to thin. The current wrote a fourth line and stopped, waiting.

The next line was new. It came in short strokes: V, E, R, A. Sára felt the sound gather in her throat though she could not call it a voice. Her dead hand, fused to the ledger, twitched on the stone. Ákos heard the name and his lullaby broke into a raw hum; the cord at his throat pulled tight, and the claimed hand on his chest trembled as if it remembered writing the same name. Márk knelt by the water and held his claimed hand under the surface. The silver trace on his palm brightened, and the cord along the stone jumped to his wrist, taut.

He did not whisper the name. He could not. The rule was plain: speaking a name cost the speaker memory, and the claimed hand bound the spoken name to the ledger. But the claimed hand could pay the toll without costing the owner memory, and it could write on blank pages, recording names and updating the toll. The water was not a page. Or maybe it was. Márk pressed his palm to the stone, and the water darkened under his hand, accepting the mark. The hidden entry wrote itself: VERA. The toll stayed at ninety-one.

Ilka looked at Sára. Sára looked at Márk's wrist. The wall-voice did not call from the corridor now; it spoke from the stone, in Sára's handwriting, though Sára had not moved her hand. "The keeper remembers," it said. "The keeper forgets."

The wall-voice's words hung in the wet air. Sára opened her mouth. Her throat worked, and for the first time in years a sound came out—thin, cracked, not a word. Ilka reached for her, but Sára lifted the dead hand fused to the ledger and shook her head. She would not spend the last of herself on a name the water already knew.

Márk looked at the blank page. "The hand writes what the mouth can't," he said. He pressed his claimed palm flat to the stone, and the cord at his wrist drew the silver trace down into the page. Letters formed in Sára's cramped script: V, E, R, A. The toll chimed but did not climb. Ninety-one held.

The moment the last letter set, the water at the ledger's foot went still. Then the murmur came again—not from the stone this time, but from the far end of the corridor above, low and patient and closer than before. "The keeper remembers," it said. "The keeper forgets. One of you will carry the name up, and one of you will leave it here."

Ákos stopped humming. "What does that mean?" he asked. No one answered him.

Ilka knelt and read the water. The old names were gone. Only VERA remained, and beneath it a fifth line was already forming, slow and deliberate, as if the river were deciding who would climb.

The fifth line did not wait for speech. It pressed down into the stone, a dark vein tracing itself along the ledger's edge, and the water at its foot gave a single, sharp ripple. Ilka paused, her fingers brushing the surface, and felt the cold shift beneath her palm. "It has chosen," she said, voice quiet but carrying across the bank. The words seemed to hang, and from the far end of the stone corridor, a breath answered: the wall-voice, now deeper, as if the stone itself were inhaling.

"One carries, one leaves," it repeated. "The name is not yours to keep."

Márk stood. The silver trace on his palm was still warm from the stone. He looked at Sára, whose dead hand remained fused to the ledger, unmoving. "You refused to spend memory," he said. "But the river does not ask for memory now. It asks for presence." He stepped toward the water, claimed hand extended. The cord at his wrist sang as the silver trace jumped, not to write, but to hold. The fifth line completed a circle around VERA, and the toll did not rise—it held at ninety-one, steady as a heartbeat.

Ákos stepped up from the corridor's mouth, his hum returning, a raw and uncertain tune. He looked between the three of them, between the ledger and the water, between the voice and the silence. His lullaby had broken, but perhaps it was not beyond repair; perhaps it was waiting for the right name to stitch itself back together. He placed his claimed hand on the stone beside Márk's, and the two cords tangled, humming in unison, as if the river's fifth line might yet name who climbs and who stays—not through cost, but through choice made visible.

The cords did not come apart. They drew tight between the two wrists, silver on silver, and where they crossed a warmth spread that neither hand had put there. It climbed Márk's arm and settled behind his eyes, and he saw a room he had not seen in months: the press-room, ink and wet paper, a boy asleep against a stack of sheets. Ákos, younger, before the lullaby broke. He remembered the weight of him on the stairs. "I know you," Márk said, and his voice cracked on it. "I carried you up when you were small. Your mother couldn't speak, so I did the talking for both of you." Ákos went still. "That's not a name I spent," he said. "You gave it back for free."

Ilka watched the water. The fifth line had not moved. "The river isn't taking," she said. "It's returning. What it holds, it gives back when two keepers stand close enough." Sára made the thin cracked sound again, and this time it bent toward a word she would not let out. Her dead hand pressed the ledger flat. The toll stayed at ninety-one.

Márk looked at the far door, then at the boy beside him. "I'll carry it up," he said. "You stay. You're the one the water can't charge—you never spent a name." Ákos opened his mouth to argue, but Sára's dead hand struck the ledger once, hard, and the sound died in him. She was staring at Márk, her cracked throat shaping the start of *no*.

Márk was already moving. He crossed to the corridor's mouth, and the fifth line pulled taut in the water, a dark thread running from the ledger's foot to his heels, as if the river had tied itself to him and meant to follow wherever he climbed.
